def get_posts(n: Union\[int, None\]=None, tags: Union\[List, None\] =
None, logged_in: bool=False): if tags: place_holders = ‘,’.join(‘?’ \*
len(tags)) private_posts_query = ’’ if logged_in else ‘AND p.private =
False’ query = f”“” SELECT DISTINCT p.\* FROM posts p JOIN post_tags pt
ON p.id = pt.post_id JOIN tags t ON pt.tag_id = t.id WHERE t.name IN
({place_holders}) AND p.published = True {private_posts_query} ORDER BY
p.created DESC ““” if n: query += f” LIMIT {n}” posts =
state.pdb.q(query, tags) else: posts =
list(state.posts_t.rows_where(“published = ? AND (private = False OR
?)”, \[True, logged_in\], order_by=“created DESC”, limit=n)) posts =
\[dict(r) for r in posts\]

    for p in posts:
        p['created'] = datetime.fromisoformat(p['created']) if isinstance(p['created'], str) else p['created']
        p['tags'] = get_post_tags(p['id'])
    return posts

``` python
@route('/admin/upload')    
def post(upload2: list[UploadFile]):
    files = [(f.filename, f.file.read()) for f in upload2]
    md_files = [(n, c) for n, c in files if n.endswith('.md')]
    img_files = [(n, c) for n, c in files if not n.endswith('.md')]
    results = []
    slug = None
    if img_files and len(md_files)==0:
        return Div(Alert("Please upload a post (.md file) with images, or upload images separately", cls=AlertT.warning))
    for name, content in md_files:
        success, message, slug = process_upload(content, name)
        results.append((name, success, message))
    for name, content in img_files:
        success, message, _ = process_upload(content, name, slug=slug)
        results.append((name, success, message))
    header = ["Name", 'Success', 'Message']
    body = [[r[0], r[1], r[2]] for r in results]
    return Div(H2("Post upload results"), TableFromLists(header, body))
```

##### 🤖Reply🤖<!-- SOLVEIT_SEPARATOR_7f3a9b2c -->

That’s a very telling observation. If both pages now trigger the bot
check — especially `test_embeds` which worked before — then YouTube has
likely flagged the shared IP range of your solveit instance due to
repeated embed requests. Nothing you can fix in code.

Moving to **bunny.net** (or similar CDN) is a solid plan. It’ll give
you:

- Full control over video delivery
- No bot checks or captchas
- Better performance and privacy for your visitors
- Ability to stream longer videos without YouTube’s restrictions

The workflow would be: 1. Upload your videos to bunny.net’s storage 2.
Use their CDN URL in your blog posts instead of YouTube URLs 3. Your
existing `process_you_tube_embed` could be adapted to produce a video

##### 🤖Reply🤖<!-- SOLVEIT_SEPARATOR_7f3a9b2c -->

Great question! The trade-off is:

- **Direct embed (like Komoot)**: simpler code, video starts loading
  with the page — better for content you want visitors to see
  immediately
- **Click-to-load thumbnail**: saves bandwidth on page load, but
  requires a click — better for performance when videos aren’t the main
  focus

For a blog, I’d lean toward the **click-to-load approach** — blog
visitors tend to scan multiple posts, and lazy-loading videos keeps page
loads snappy. But it’s really your call based on how you use videos in
your posts.

Shall we start with the simpler approach (direct embed, matching
Komoot’s pattern) and you can decide later if you want to optimize
further?

##### 🤖Reply🤖<!-- SOLVEIT_SEPARATOR_7f3a9b2c -->

Good question! In bunny.net, the flow is:

1.  **Storage Zone** — this is where you upload your video files (like
    FTP). You get a storage URL and an API key/username+password.
2.  **Pull Zone** — this is the CDN endpoint that serves your files to
    visitors. You connect it to your storage zone as the “origin”.

So the steps are:

- Create a **Storage Zone** (e.g. `my-blog-videos`) — upload your .mp4
  files there via FTP or their dashboard
- Create a **Pull Zone** that pulls from that storage zone — you’ll get
  a CDN URL like `https://my-blog-videos.b-cdn.net`
- Then in your blog, you can serve
  `https://my-blog-videos.b-cdn.net/grassington.mp4`

You don’t need to keep the files on your own server — bunny stores them
and serves them via their CDN.

Does that help? Want to give it a try creating a storage zone?

Which type of video files with most browsers work with. I know .mp4 is
ok, any others

##### 🤖Reply🤖<!-- SOLVEIT_SEPARATOR_7f3a9b2c -->

The big three that work across all modern browsers:

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 22%" />
<col style="width: 51%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Format</th>
<th>Codec</th>
<th>Browser support</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>.mp4</strong></td>
<td>H.264</td>
<td>Universal — everything supports it</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>.webm</strong></td>
<td>VP8/VP9</td>
<td>Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Opera (not Safari natively)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>.ogg/.ogv</strong></td>
<td>Theora</td>
<td>Firefox, Chrome, Edge (dropped by Safari)</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

For practical purposes, **.mp4** is the safe choice — it works
everywhere and bunny.net will serve it just fine. If you want to be
thorough, you can supply both an mp4 and webm version in a `<video>`
element with multiple `<source>` tags, but that’s overkill for a blog.

Stick with mp4 and you’re good. Want to draft your embedding function
now?

##### 🤖Reply🤖<!-- SOLVEIT_SEPARATOR_7f3a9b2c -->

Good call — since you set `width="100%"` on the `<video>` tag, the
browser **will** adapt it to the width of its container (the blog post
area). The height will scale proportionally based on the video’s aspect
ratio automatically.

The `controls` attribute also gives the user play/pause, volume, and
fullscreen controls, so on mobile they can go fullscreen if needed.
